introduction-why-default-settings-are-wr.core: Linux TCP defaults are tuned for generic, modest networks. On high-bandwidth, high-latency links (cross-region replication, CDN origins, backups), small default buffers cap throughput far below link capacity, the default congestion control may react poorly to loss, and deep queues cause bufferbloat. Tuning means matching buffers to the bandwidth-delay product, choosing congestion control, and managing queues.

first_principles.problem: A 10 Gbps link between US and EU regions moves a single stream at 300 Mbps.

analogy.title: A pipeline with a small tap
analogy.story: A huge, long pipeline stays mostly empty if the tap at the start only lets a trickle in.
analogy.breaks: Water doesn't need acknowledgements; TCP does.

code.text:
ping -c 10 10.20.0.5 | tail -1          # RTT ~80 ms
iperf3 -c 10.20.0.5 -t 20               # ~300 Mbits/sec
ss -ti dst 10.20.0.5 | grep -E 'cwnd|rtt|wscale'

check.q: Why doesn't a faster link automatically speed up a single TCP stream?
check.a: Throughput is capped by window size divided by RTT, so small windows limit speed regardless of link capacity.

bandwidth-delay-product-bdp.core: The bandwidth-delay product is how much data must be in flight to keep a link full: bandwidth × RTT. A 10 Gbps link with 80 ms RTT needs 10e9 × 0.08 / 8 = 100 MB in flight. If the sender's or receiver's window (bounded by socket buffers) is smaller, the link idles between ACKs. BDP sets the buffer sizes needed for full throughput.

first_principles.problem: Engineers don't know how big to make TCP buffers for a cross-ocean link.
truths: Data in flight equals rate × time.

analogy.title: Cars needed to fill a motorway
analogy.story: A longer, wider motorway needs more cars on it at once to be fully used.
analogy.breaks: Cars don't need return trips; ACKs must come back before more data is sent.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Autotuning can grow windows to fill the pipe.

code.text:
# 10 Gbps × 0.08 s / 8 = 100 MB → allow up to 128 MB
sysctl -w net.core.rmem_max=134217728 net.core.wmem_max=134217728
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 131072 134217728'
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_wmem='4096 65536 134217728'

check.q: What is the BDP for a 1 Gbps link with 20 ms RTT?

tcp-window-scaling.core: The TCP header's window field is 16 bits, so the maximum is 65,535 bytes, far below modern BDPs. Window scaling (RFC 7323), negotiated in the SYN, adds a shift count of up to 14 that multiplies the advertised window by up to 2^14, allowing about 1 GB windows. It must be enabled on both ends and survive middleboxes, which have historically stripped or mangled the option.

first_principles.problem: Throughput is stuck at ~6 Mbps on a 80 ms link because a middlebox strips the window scale option.
truths: The scale factor is negotiated once.

analogy.title: Using 'thousands' units on a small display
analogy.story: A counter that shows only 5 digits can show millions if everyone agrees it's in thousands.
analogy.breaks: Displays don't get edited mid-route; middleboxes can strip options.

code.text:
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_window_scaling      # 1
ss -ti dst 10.20.0.5 | grep -o 'wscale:[0-9,]*'
# wscale:9,9  → windows multiplied by 512
tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' -v | grep wscale

check.q: Why must window scaling be negotiated in the SYN?
check.a: Both sides must agree on the shift factor at connection start; it can't be changed later.

tcp-congestion-control-algorithms.core: Congestion control decides how fast to send. Reno and NewReno halve the window on loss and grow linearly. CUBIC, the Linux default, grows as a cubic function and recovers faster on high-BDP paths but still treats loss as congestion. BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and RTT, pacing at the estimated rate regardless of random loss, which greatly improves throughput on lossy long paths, though fairness with CUBIC flows needs care.

first_principles.problem: A transfer over a path with 0.1% random loss gets 20% of link capacity with CUBIC.

analogy.title: Driving by brake lights vs by measuring road capacity
analogy.story: CUBIC brakes whenever it sees a brake light (loss); BBR estimates the road's speed limit and cruises at it.
analogy.breaks: Drivers see other cars; algorithms infer from ACKs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Lossy long path throughput rises dramatically.

code.text:
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control
sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
iperf3 -c 10.20.0.5 -C bbr -t 20

check.q: Why does BBR outperform CUBIC on paths with random loss?
check.a: CUBIC interprets every loss as congestion and backs off; BBR paces by estimated bandwidth and RTT, largely ignoring non-congestive loss.

bufferbloat-the-latency-killer.core: Bufferbloat is excessive buffering in routers, modems and hosts. Loss-based TCP fills any buffer before seeing loss, so a large queue at the bottleneck holds seconds of data, and latency for everything else (calls, games, DNS) explodes under load even though throughput looks fine. The fix isn't bigger buffers but smarter queue management that keeps queues short.

first_principles.problem: Video calls freeze whenever someone in the house uploads a large file, though bandwidth tests look good.
derivation: Shape slightly **below link rate** to own the queue.

analogy.title: A long queue at a single checkout
analogy.story: The cashier is always busy (good throughput), but someone with one item waits 20 minutes.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers can switch queues; packets can't.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proves queueing delay, not bandwidth, is the problem.

code.text:
ping -i 0.2 8.8.8.8 &          # idle ~15 ms
iperf3 -c server -R -t 30      # saturate download
# ping rises to 800+ ms → bufferbloat

check.q: Why doesn't buying more bandwidth always fix bufferbloat?
check.a: The bottleneck still has an oversized queue that loss-based TCP fills; latency depends on queue length, not raw speed.

fighting-bufferbloat-codel-and-fq_codel.core: CoDel (Controlled Delay) watches how long packets sit in the queue. If the minimum sojourn time stays above about 5 ms for an interval of about 100 ms, it starts dropping (or ECN-marking) to signal senders to slow down, keeping queues short without tuning by size. fq_codel adds fair queuing, giving each flow its own queue, so a bulk upload can't starve small flows. CAKE adds shaping and more for home routers.

first_principles.problem: A router must keep latency low for calls while uploads saturate the link.
truths: Delay, not size, is the right signal.

analogy.title: A supermarket manager watching wait times
analogy.story: If people wait over 5 minutes, open a separate lane for small baskets and tell bulk shoppers to slow down.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers comply; TCP responds only if it sees signals.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Ping under load stays near idle latency.

code.text:
tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root fq_codel
# or with shaping for a 100 Mbit uplink:
tc qdisc replace dev eth0 root cake bandwidth 95mbit
tc -s qdisc show dev eth0

check.q: Why shape slightly below the link rate when applying fq_codel/CAKE?
check.a: So the queue forms in your managed qdisc instead of the modem/ISP's unmanaged buffer.

tcp-fast-open-tfo.core: A normal TCP connection spends one full RTT on the handshake before sending data. TCP Fast Open lets a returning client send data in the SYN, using a cookie the server issued on an earlier connection, so the server can respond immediately, saving one RTT. It needs client and server support and middleboxes that don't drop SYNs carrying data, and replayed SYN data means the first request should be idempotent.

first_principles.problem: Short API calls from mobile clients spend half their latency on TCP handshakes.
truths: Previously seen clients can be trusted with a cookie.

analogy.title: A regular customer phoning in their order while walking in
analogy.story: The barista recognises them (cookie) and starts the coffee before formal greetings.
analogy.breaks: Baristas spot impostors; replayed SYNs can repeat the order.

example.title: Enable and test

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Repeat connections send request with SYN.

example.outcome: one RTT saved for repeat clients.

check.q: Why should TFO's first request be idempotent?
check.a: SYN data can be replayed or duplicated, so processing it twice must be harmless.

putting-it-all-together-a-tuning-checkli.core: Tune systematically. Measure baseline RTT, throughput and latency under load; compute the BDP and raise rmem/wmem maxima (with window scaling on); choose BBR plus fq for long or lossy paths, CUBIC otherwise; use fq_codel or CAKE where queues form; enable TFO or connection reuse for short flows; check MTU and offloads; then re-measure and roll out gradually, since every setting has trade-offs.

first_principles.problem: A team changes ten sysctls at once, performance worsens, and nobody knows which change caused it.

analogy.title: Tuning a race car
analogy.story: Change one setting per lap and time it; changing everything at once tells you nothing.
analogy.breaks: Race tracks are consistent; production traffic varies.

code.text:
# /etc/sysctl.d/90-wan-tuning.conf
net.core.rmem_max = 134217728
net.core.wmem_max = 134217728
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 131072 134217728
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 134217728
net.core.default_qdisc = fq
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = bbr
net.ipv4.tcp_fastopen = 3
net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing = 1

check.q: Why change only one TCP setting at a time?
check.a: Settings interact; isolating changes shows which one helped or hurt.
